To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the use of orthodox statistical tests to make decisions as to how one should behave is philosophically unjustifiable; (b) orthodox tests are, however, appropriate and justified as learning tools; and (c) the learning model of tests is philosophically superior to the decision model.

(1) a test of the hypothesis that the population mean is 100, using a sample mean of 98, is significant at the 0.05 level, and (2) a test of a hypothesis of the same kind, using a sample of the same size, and a sample mean of the same value, is not significant at the 5% level.

(1) the test is not a behavioral decision rule; (2) it does not provide a measure of evidential strength for a hypothesis; (3) it is not a rule for choosing among hypotheses; (4) it does not tell us whether a given hypothesis should or should not be rejected; and (5) it is a rule for learning about the process that produced the observed data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of what is the appropriate model for statistical testing, and how this model is related to the question of what constitutes evidence.
the question: "How can statistical tests provide a basis for the acquisition of scientific knowledge?"
the nature and role of probability in scientific inference.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
statistical tests, as typically understood and applied, are not appropriate for making decisions as to how one should behave.
orthodox statistical tests are not rules for making optimal behavioral decisions or for assigning measures of evidential support.
the orthodox tests are not the only way to learn, but they do a good job of it.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the orthodox statistical tests are not appropriate for evidential purposes.

we have provided a new model for interpreting the results of statistical tests, a model that is more consistent with the way statistical tests are used in science and that is also consistent with the philosophical views of most philosophers of statistics.
we provide a new model for statistical testing that is consistent with the orthodox model and the evidential model.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the controversy over orthodox tests is not about tests per se, but about the task they are used to accomplish.
the controversy over orthodox statistical testing is a false dichotomy between behavioral-decision and evidentialist models.
statistical testing is a tool for learning about processes that generate data.
